name: The Beveridge Curve
statement: The Beveridge curve shows an inverse relationship between the unemployment rate and the job vacancy rate across the business cycle.
statementAccent: inverse relationship between the unemployment rate and the job vacancy rate
meaning: The Beveridge curve, or UV curve, plots the job vacancy rate against the unemployment rate for an economy over time. It typically slopes downward: when unemployment is high, vacancies tend to be low (recessions), and when unemployment is low, vacancies tend to be high (expansions). Movements along the curve reflect the business cycle, while shifts of the whole curve indicate changes in labour-market matching efficiency.
mechanism: The curve emerges from worker flows into and out of unemployment and job flows into and out of vacancy: in a slump, weak demand raises unemployment and firms post fewer openings; in a boom, strong demand lowers unemployment while firms post more openings competing for scarcer workers. Its position shifts outward when matching between seekers and vacancies worsens — through skills mismatch, reduced recruiting intensity, or longer unemployment spells.

examples.text: The curve is named for British economist William Beveridge, whose 1944 book "Full Employment in a Free Society" argued unemployment fluctuations were driven by labour-demand fluctuations; economists Christopher Dow and Leslie Dicks-Mireaux plotted the first graphical version in 1958 using British data.

Using US JOLTS data, the Beveridge curve shifted outward from late 2007, with vacancies recovering while unemployment fell only sluggishly — a pattern Federal Reserve researchers linked to skill mismatch, reduced recruiting intensity, and rising long-term unemployment.

A San Francisco Fed analysis noted that in May 2022 US unemployment stood at 3.6% while the vacancy rate reached 7.2%, and used the curve’s shape to model whether vacancies could fall without a large rise in unemployment.

whyItMatters: The curve is a standard diagnostic for central banks and labour economists to judge whether the labour market is tight or slack, and whether high unemployment reflects insufficient demand or worsened matching — a distinction central to monetary policy.
limits: The simple inverse relationship can shift for reasons unrelated to cyclical demand, such as changing participation, extended benefits, or persistent sectoral mismatch, so a shift requires careful interpretation rather than a single explanation. Recent research documents nonlinearities rather than a fixed, stable curve.
misreadings: An outward shift is sometimes wrongly read as proof that unemployed workers are unwilling to work, when the standard interpretation attributes it to changes in matching efficiency, mismatch, or recruiting behaviour on both sides of the market.
origin: Named after economist William Beveridge (from ideas in his 1944 "Full Employment in a Free Society"); first plotted graphically by Christopher Dow and L. A. Dicks-Mireaux in 1958 using UK data.

sources.text: Beveridge curve, Wikipedia. — the definition, origin, mechanism, and Great Recession and COVID shifts.
Federal Reserve Bank of San Francisco, "Finding a Soft Landing along the Beveridge Curve" (2022). — the 2022 US unemployment/vacancy data and policy use of the curve.
